title: Guided Notes

vocab.Population: The entire group the question is about --- every individual you would like the conclusion to describe. Decided by the question, not by who is available.
vocab.Sample: The part of the population you actually collected data from. The number of individuals in it is the sample size, $n$.
vocab.Parameter: A number that describes the population. Usually unknown --- and there is exactly one of it, whether or not anyone has ever computed it.
vocab.Statistic: A number computed from the sample. Known, because you collected the data --- and it changes from one sample to the next.
vocab.Sampling variability: The change in a statistic from one sample to the next, even though the population did not change. Not a mistake --- it is what samples do.

lines: Answers vary --- most of the room picks a volunteer, or says the truth is ``in between.''
(Settled at problem 14: nobody --- three samples, three statistics, one parameter.)
spaces: Each asked a different 50 shoppers, so each got a different statistic. The one parameter never moved.

cells.1: Population: all 800 Saturday shoppers. Sample: the 50 asked. $n = 50$.
cells.2: Population: all 900 Riverbend students. Sample: the 45 asked. $n = 45$.
cells.3: Population: the 12,000 boxes filled Tuesday. Sample: the 30 weighed. $n = 30$.
cells.4: Population: all 800 shoppers. Sample: the same 800 --- the sample is the whole population: a census.
cells.6: Describes all 800 shoppers --- a parameter (a count, and still a parameter).
cells.8: Describes all 900 students --- a parameter, even though it is a percent.
cells.10: Access (or time) --- shoppers leave before she can reach them.
cells.11: Run a census --- ask all 800. Time and access forbid it.
cells.13: Three statistics --- one from each sample. One true percent: there is exactly one parameter for all 800.
cells.14: Nobody. Nobody counted wrong, and none found the true percent --- three estimates of one parameter.
cells.15: Usually closer, but not exactly on it every time --- it is still a statistic.
cells.16: Population: Riverbend's 900 students. Sample: the 50 she asked; $n = 50$. Constraint: time (or cost, access).
cells.17: $20/50 = 0.40 = 40\%$ --- a statistic. \par $0.40 \times 900 = 360$ --- an estimate of the parameter.
cells.18: $23/50 = 0.46 = 46\%$. No mistake --- two samples, two statistics. Neither found it: one parameter, both estimate it.
cells.19: No --- 360 was computed from the 40\%, not counted. ``Of the 50 asked, 40\% have a job; that is about 360 of the 900.''
